c.tagline: The City of Eternal Spring, reborn through cable cars and creativity.

taxi.fareNote: Yellow street taxis run on a meter (tarifa), with a night and airport surcharge. Many travelers instead book through Cabify, DiDi or Uber for an app-tracked yellow taxi or private car.

emergency.note: 123 is Colombia's free, 24/7 unified emergency line connecting to police, ambulance and fire. 112 reaches the National Police even with no SIM credit or while roaming; 125 is the ambulance line and 119 the fire department.

solo.f: Safety index is the main factor (46/100)

avoid.reason: Visit Comuna 13 only on organised tours; avoid unlit comunas at night.
Drink-spiking and robbery around El Poblado’s nightlife — watch your drink.

hood_desc: Medellín's upscale hillside tourist heart around Parque Lleras, Provenza and Manila, packed with rooftop bars, restaurants, cafes and boutique hotels; where most first-timers base themselves, though it can be pricey and noisy at night.

A flat, leafy, grid-planned residential barrio of tree-lined streets, the La 70 and La 33 dining strips and a genuine local feel; a safe, walkable favorite of digital nomads wanting an authentic stay.

The gritty, energetic historic downtown around Plaza Botero, the Museo de Antioquia and Parque Berrío; a major transit hub full of sculptures, street markets and colonial churches by day, but best avoided after dark.
An independent traditional town on Medellín's south side with a lively main plaza, family-run eateries and a relaxed, authentically paisa pace; popular with long-stay expats living like locals.

The smallest municipality in the Aburrá Valley by area, on Medellín's southern edge and on the metro's A line, centred on a pretty church plaza famous for chuzos street food and a calm, small-town feel loved by locals and remote workers.

water.note: EPM-treated tap water is safe to drink in the metro area.

transit.hours: The Metro runs roughly 4:30am-11:00pm on weekdays, until about 11:30pm on Saturdays and shorter hours on Sundays and holidays; ride apps and taxis cover the late-night gap.
transit.note: The Medellín Metro is clean, cheap, safe and a point of local pride; its Metrocable cable-car lines double as everyday transport up the steep hillside barrios and to Parque Arví, offering some of the best city views.
transit.pay: Visitors tap a rechargeable Cívica smart card (free/cheap to obtain and top up at station windows) covering the Metro, Tranvía, Metrocable and integrated buses with free transfers; single-ride paper tickets are also sold at station booths in cash.

tip.r: A 10% 'propina voluntaria' (voluntary service charge) is usually added to restaurant bills — you'll be asked '¿servicio incluido?' and can accept, adjust or decline it.

food.name: Bandeja paisa
food.desc: The Antioquian tray: red beans, rice, chicharron, ground beef, chorizo, morcilla, fried egg, plantain, arepa and avocado. One plate, one afternoon.

places.name: Mondongos
places.note: The name locals give first for bandeja paisa; the Laureles original is the one to hit.

places.name: Hatoviejo
places.note: Paisa institution since 1982, cited by TasteAtlas as a benchmark for the dish.

places.name: La Matriarca
places.note: Modern room two blocks from Parque Poblado doing the full traditional tray.

food.name: Mondongo
food.desc: Slow-simmered tripe soup with potato, carrot and chorizo, finished at the table with lime, coriander and a spoon of hot rice.

places.name: Mondongos
places.note: Named for the soup and still the reference version in the city.

places.name: Hatoviejo
places.note: Serves mondongo alongside sancocho antioqueno and regional tamales.

places.name: La Matriarca
places.note: Keeps mondongo, ajiaco and cazuela de frijoles on the everyday menu.

food.name: Arepa paisa
food.desc: Thin white-corn arepa, no salt, griddled and slathered with butter and salty quesito. The Antioquian answer to bread.

places.name: Mercado del Rio
places.note: Food hall with several arepa counters, good for comparing styles in one stop.

places.name: Plaza Minorista Jose Maria Villa
places.note: Working market where arepas come off the griddle beside the produce stalls.

places.name: Mondongos
places.note: Arepas arrive with almost everything; good place to try the plain paisa version.

food.name: Chicharron
food.desc: A slab of pork belly fried until the skin shatters and the meat underneath stays juicy. Ordered on its own as much as on the tray.

places.name: Hatoviejo
places.note: Traditional kitchen that treats chicharron as a headline item, not a garnish.

places.name: Mondongos
places.note: Reliable, generously cut chicharron at prices locals still pay.

places.name: Mercado del Rio
places.note: Several stalls fry chicharron to order in the covered market hall.

food.name: Sancocho antioqueno
food.desc: Beef rib or chicken boiled down with yuca, plantain and corn into a hearty Sunday soup, served with rice and avocado on the side.

places.name: Hatoviejo
places.note: Sancocho is one of its signature regional plates.

places.name: La Matriarca
places.note: Antioquian classics including sancocho and ajiaco in a comfortable setting.

places.name: Mondongos
places.note: Soup-focused menu with sancocho and cazuela de lentejas beside the mondongo.

food.name: Bunuelos y natilla
food.desc: Round cheese-dough fritters fried golden, paired with cinnamon-scented natilla custard. Christmas food that Medellin eats year-round.

places.name: Pasteleria Astor
places.note: Medellin pastry institution since the 1960s, strong on traditional sweets.

places.name: Versalles
places.note: Old-school downtown cafe-bakery, a fixture for pastries and coffee since 1963.

places.name: Mercado del Rio
places.note: Dessert counters selling bunuelos, natilla and obleas under one roof.

food.name: Aguardiente Antioqueno
food.desc: Anise-flavoured sugarcane spirit, sold by the bottle with a stack of shot glasses. Sharing it is the point, not the taste.

places.name: Salon Malaga
places.note: Historic tango and bolero bar where the aguardiente comes with vinyl records.

places.name: Mercado del Rio
places.note: Central bars in the food hall pour it by the shot or half bottle.

places.name: Hatoviejo
places.note: Traditional restaurant where a bottle on the table is standard practice.

food.name: Cafe de origen
food.desc: Antioquian single-origin coffee, the good beans that used to all be exported. Ask for a filter pour-over, not the sweet street tinto.

places.name: Pergamino Cafe
places.note: Farm-to-cup roaster widely credited with starting Medellin specialty coffee scene.

places.name: Cafe Velvet
places.note: Small roastery-cafe with rotating Colombian single origins and careful brewing.

places.name: Salon Malaga
places.note: Old-Medellin cafe for a traditional tinto in the middle of downtown.

landmarks: Plaza Botero
This open-air plaza displays 23 monumental bronze sculptures donated by native son Fernando Botero, making it one of the most photographed spots in the city.
Comuna 13 Graffiti Tour
Once one of the most dangerous neighborhoods in the world, its outdoor escalators and vibrant street art now tell a powerful story of transformation.
Metrocable
This aerial cable-car system was the first of its kind built to serve hillside neighborhoods, offering sweeping views over the entire valley.
Pueblito Paisa
A charming replica of a traditional Antioquian village perched atop Cerro Nutibara, delivering panoramic views of the city below.
Catedral Metropolitana
One of the largest brick-built cathedrals in the world, its massive red-brick facade dominates Parque Bolívar.
Palacio de la Cultura Rafael Uribe Uribe
A striking Flemish Gothic-style cultural palace with colorful mosaic facades designed with input from Fernando Botero.
Parque Arví
A vast nature reserve reached via a scenic cable-car ride, popular for hiking, picnics, and escaping the city into cloud forest.
Jardín Botánico de Medellín
A lush botanical garden in the heart of the city, famous for its lakeside orchid pavilion (Orquideorama) and tropical greenery.
Parque Explora
An interactive science museum and aquarium with a bold, vividly colored modern building that stands out on the skyline.
Museo de Antioquia
A historic art museum with the world's largest collection of Botero works, set in a grand early-20th-century building beside Plaza Botero.

train.note: Colombia has no scheduled intercity passenger rail, so there are no trains between cities from Medellín. The city's Metro - the only one in Colombia - plus its Metrocable gondolas are urban transit and worth riding for the views over the valley. Travel between cities is by coach or plane.

intl.to: Quito (Ecuador) & Lima (Peru) - long-haul services via Ipiales

bus.note: Medellín has two terminals: Terminal del Norte for Cartagena, Santa Marta and the coast, Terminal del Sur for Bogotá, Cali and the coffee region. Bogotá takes about 9-10 hours and Cartagena 13. The international runs to Ecuador and Peru are multi-day journeys crossing at Ipiales/Rumichaca - carry your passport. Book through Pinbus (https://pinbus.com/) or at the terminals.

ferry.note: Medellín sits in a mountain valley at 1,500 m with no navigable water, so there are no ferries. Boats on the Guatapé reservoir, about two hours east, are day-trip excursions.

half.name: Santa Fe de Antioquia
half.blurb: A colonial town under an hour away via the Occidente tunnel, with whitewashed 16th-century streets and a suspension bridge.

full.name: Guatapé
full.blurb: A colorful lakeside town about two and a half hours away, known for the Piedra del Peñol monolith and its 740-step climb.

laundry.note: Drop-off per kilo is the norm, 24h turnaround
